name: Daily Montanan
title: Another lawsuit filed over 2025 property tax legislation
text:
Photo illustration by Getty Images.Three current and former legislators have filed another lawsuit over Senate Bill 542, a property tax bill signed last year.
State Sen. Greg Hertz, Senate Majority Leader Tom McGillvray and former legislator Keith Regier, all Republicans, jointly filed the lawsuit this week saying SB 542 violates the constitution’s equal protection clause. 
Under SB 542, residential property tax rates differ depending on their market value. The lawsuit, which was filed in Gallatin County, says setting different rates within the same property class violates the constitution.
“Tax relief for one group of Montanans should not come at the expense of unfairly taxing their neighbors. The Montana Constitution protects equal treatment, and we are asking the courts to enforce those protections,” McGillvray said in a press release. “This lawsuit is not about opposing property tax relief. It is about ensuring that tax relief is provided in a manner that respects the constitutional rights of every Montana property owner.”
The lawsuit says equal protection clauses protect individuals from “state action which selects him or her out for discriminatory treatment by subjecting him or her to taxes not imposed on others of the same class.”
Hertz, McGillvray and Regier previously filed a suit over the bill, saying it violated the constitution’s single-subject rule, which says a bill must address just one topic, and it must be clear. That suit, which the state GOP joined on the side of the plaintiffs, is still pending and was also filed in Gallatin County District Court.
“Montanans deserve a property tax system that is fair, transparent, and constitutional,” Hertz said in a press release. “The Legislature has the authority to establish property classifications, but once property is placed within the same class, the constitution requires that taxpayers be treated equally.”
SB 542 was passed during the 2025 session and signed into law by Republican Gov. Greg Gianforte. Some legislators referred to it as a “Frankstein” bill during the sessions, as it drew heavily from other legislation that didn’t pass.
The Governor’s Office did not immediately comment on the suit, but has expressed support for the legislation, saying 80% of Montanans got property tax relief.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Legislators say Laurel could be breaking federal law
text:
Signs line the lawn of the Laurel Public Library as community resident gather before a listening session on a proposed state psychiatric facility. The meeting happened on April 22, 2026 (Photo by Darrell Ehrlick of the Daily Montanan). Montana legislators accused the City of Laurel of potentially breaking federal law in a fight over a mental health facility outside of the city in a meeting and a letter to the local government earlier this month.
Legislators in the Long Range Planning Interim Budget Committee also threatened to withhold municipal funding following a moratorium Laurel unanimously passed last month that halted annexing any land so it can study the city’s water system. Those issues also include aging infrastructure, fire protection problems and areas of low water pressure. There’s also been problems with the city’s water intake from the Yellowstone River.
State plans call for building a 32-bed mental health facility at the edge of Laurel city limits in Yellowstone County. Laurel residents have pushed back on the proposal citing problems they say could arise when the facility is built, including concerns the city’s utilities won’t be able to keep up.
City officials say they pressed pause on annexation applications so Laurel can study its water system. Some legislators, meanwhile, say the city is discriminating against those with mental illnesses and could be breaking federal law.  
A letter sent from the Long Range Planning Interim Budget Committee to Laurel and Montana’s congressional delegation says the city’s decision “essentially means the city will not provide water service to the proposed new mental health facility for forensic patients” and goes on to say the ordinance was “discriminatory.” 
State officials decided during the summer to place the facility outside Laurel. Onsite work at the facility has been paused while a lawsuit over the construction proceeds.
The letter from legislators to the City of Laurel says the action “may subject” the city to a lawsuit for violating federal law. Legislators unanimously approved the letter during an Oct. 8 committee meeting. 
Additionally, during that meeting, legislators by a 4-3 vote approved a “global motion” to direct the legislature to consider not directing any funding to any municipality under investigation for violations to the Americans with Disability Act, the Fair Housing Act or the Montana Human Rights Act.
The vote does not immediately strip any municipalities of any funding but means the issue of whether cities under federal investigation are eligible for state money will be taken up by the Legislative Finance Committee when it resumes during the 2027 session. Laurel was the only city discussed during the meeting.
“The legislature is not going to investigate the city of Laurel,” said John Esp, a Big Timber Republican and chairperson of the committee. “Somebody’s going to file a complaint on fair housing grounds, or on Americans with Disabilities grounds, or with the Montana Human Rights Commission, and while they’re under investigation by the Human Rights Commission or some federal agency, that’s when the prohibition on getting state money kicks in.”
Any sort of penalties wouldn’t begin unless the Legislature passes a bill to that effect next session.
When asked if any complaints have been filed against the City of Laurel, a Department of Labor and Industries employee within the Montana Human Rights Bureau directed the Daily Montanan to file a records request, which it has done. Federal Fair Housing Act violations would fall within the  U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, while Americans with Disabilities Act violations are investigated by a variety of federal entities.
In a five-page response to the lawmaker’s letter, Laurel Mayor Kris Vogele said he disagrees with the legislators, and expressed concern about any potential loss of funding. Some legislators worried the motion could negatively impact cities that are under investigation but end up not having broken federal law. Laurel receives millions of dollars in state funding per year, though city officials said they weren’t sure how much. 
For example, per the Montana League of Cities and Towns documentation, cities are projected to receive about $26 million in roads funding from the state, which is protected by statute. Laurel is projected to receive about $300,000 from that funding stream.
The legislative motion made by Sen. Ellie Boldman, a Missoula Democrat, said “that the legislature not consider or fund any local government request while under investigation for discriminating against a state facility.”
“Our intent right here on this call is to encourage the City of Laurel to take a look at this on their own,” Boldman said during the meeting, “so that nobody has to withhold anything.”
In a separate email to media members, Vogele said the committee was advancing a “deeply troubling allegation.”
“These are extraordinarily serious accusations, made with potentially far-reaching consequences not only for Laurel, but for communities across Montana,” Vogele wrote in a statement. “An investigation is not a finding of wrongdoing. An allegation is not proof of discrimination. And a Montana community should not risk losing state funding simply because its elected officials raise legitimate questions about whether its infrastructure can safely support a major state project.”
The Laurel response also references a 95-page document the city sent the state regarding its environmental assessment of the mental health facility property. That document, sent to the state in September, asks for more assessment of the site “to establish a complete and supportable record.” 
The mental health facility has been an issue in Laurel for more than a year, and some residents have also expressed worry about the impacts to the city’s sewer and water systems, while others have been concerned about its location within a mile of an elementary school.

name: California
title: California’s ballot propositions fuel its longstanding tax-and-spending war
text:
California voters will pass judgment on 14 statewide ballot measures this year and all but two of them relate, in some manner, to financing public services.
Collectively they represent the latest version of what fiscal policy buffs call “ballot box budgeting” — persuading voters to prioritize or limit how funds are raised and spent rather than leaving those issues to elected officials.
This election’s most contentious measure, Proposition 40, typifies the underlying philosophical conflict that has raged ever since voters passed Proposition 13, the state’s iconic limit on property taxes, nearly a half-century ago.
Prop. 13 embodied the belief that high taxes undercut Californians’ ability to enhance the welfare of their own families. Prop. 40, which would impose a 5% tax on the wealth of California’s billionaires, reflects the counter-contention that expansive public services better serve the well-being of all Californians.
Before Prop. 13 made the June 1978 ballot, the initiative process almost never dealt with tax and spending issues, a yearly summary from the secretary of state’s office indicates. Implicitly, voters were content to leave such money matters to elected state and local officials.
Prop. 13 reduced property taxes that had been the fundamental revenue source for local governments and school systems. It also made raising taxes of all kinds more difficult.
Prop. 13’s jolting impact also encouraged the use of ballot measures process not only to affect public finance issues but policies of all kinds. Succeeding elections saw an explosion of proposals dealing with such issues as punishment for crimes, immigration, affirmative action and same-sex marriage.
The two measures on this year’s ballot that don’t deal with taxes and spending typify that trend. Proposition 39 would require voters to show identifying documents and Proposition 45 would reduce use of the California Environmental Quality Act to block projects.
However, taxes and spending continued to dominate post-Prop. 13 elections, beginning in 1979 with a special election called by then-Gov. Jerry Brown to pass Proposition 4, a cap on state spending known as the “Gann Limit” for Paul Gann, a co-author of Prop. 13 with fellow tax gadfly Howard Jarvis.
Brown had strenuously opposed Prop. 13 but after its passage declared himself to be a “born-again tax cutter” and joined with Gann to persuade voters to approve the spending limit. It continues to be a factor in fashioning an annual state budget.
A much bigger budget factor is Proposition 98, a 1988 measure sponsored by the California Teachers Association to cushion Prop. 13’s impact on school finances. Prop. 98 contains a complex formula to guarantee a certain level of state education aid that works out to about 40% of general fund revenues.
The teachers’ union is opposing this year’s Prop. 40, the wealth tax on billionaires, which designates all but a small percentage of its revenue for healthcare, excluding Prop. 98. The conflict illustrates how ballot box budgeting pits interest groups against each other, even those on the same side in their underlying battle with anti-tax forces.
Speaking of which, anti-tax groups such as the Howard Jarvis Taxpayers Association have continued to press their cause, staving off efforts to change Prop. 13 and promoting tax limits.
This year, they are pushing Proposition 43, which would increase the vote requirement to approve some local taxes. And they’re opposing the California Teachers Association’s Proposition 3, which would make permanent a temporary tax on high-income Californians that was initially passed in 2012 at Brown’s behest during his second stint as governor.
During the 17th century, a conflict known as the 30 Years War raged in Europe. Today California’s war over taxes and spending is already 48 years old and, as this year’s array of ballot measures indicates, it shows no sign of ending.

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Increases in farm building assessments fuel calls to revisit Indiana’s property valuation system
text:
A wind turbine near a rural Indiana farm in September 2026. (Photo by Niki Kelly/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana farmers facing steep increases in building assessments are calling for changes to the state’s property valuation system, warning lawmakers Wednesday that similar structures are being assessed differently across county lines.
Indiana Farm Bureau representatives told the Interim Study Committee on Fiscal Policy that updated state cost tables have pushed up the assessed values of barns, grain bins and livestock facilities ahead of next year’s tax bills.
They urged lawmakers to address those discrepancies rather than leave individual property owners to challenge their assessments.
State officials acknowledged the concerns but cautioned that assessment changes alone would not resolve complaints about rising tax bills. They instead recommended preserving annual adjustments while improving assessment data and testing automated valuation tools.
Lawmakers also raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments climb as new or renovated houses change the surrounding market, and questioned whether new technology could help catch errors before taxpayers have to appeal.
The committee additionally heard an update on Indiana’s childcare voucher programs and proposals to finance expanded access ahead of the 2027 budget session. Discussions focused on sustaining the state’s recent voucher expansion and drawing more investment from employers, philanthropy and local governments.
Farm building increases draw concerns
Katrina Hall, Indiana Farm Bureau’s senior director of policy strategy and advocacy, said the organization commissioned Policy Analytics to examine agricultural building assessments after members began reporting large increases earlier this year.
The analysis initially showed a statewide increase of about 44% in assessed value for the agricultural buildings studied, she said. Later data, reflecting appeals and discussions with assessors, reduced that increase to 29% — still about $2 billion in additional assessed value for taxes payable in 2027.
More than half of the parcels in the later analysis had increases of at least 15%, Hall said. The figures show how much assessed values increased, not how much farmers’ tax bills will rise.
Story continues below.
attachment_6377
 
Hall said the discrepancies suggest a problem with statewide consistency. Some assessors made adjustments to the cost tables, she said, while others appeared to use them without similar changes. Identical buildings of the same age can consequently receive different values in neighboring counties.
She argued that appeals cannot substitute for correcting the underlying assessment process.
“Appeals are like a parcel at a time,” Hall said. “They are not fixing problems with assessing in the tax base.”
Farm Bureau wants the state to consider a nationally recognized valuation system, like Marshall & Swift, and examine outdated depreciation schedules. Hall said taxpayers seeking to challenge assessments often get appraisals using that system, creating a mismatch with the state’s tools.
The organization also proposed moving agricultural improvements from the 3% property tax cap category to the 2% category. Hall said its analysis estimated about $44 million in savings across agricultural properties.
That would be a tax relief change separate from revisions to assessment methods.
The proposals follow Indiana’s 2025 property tax overhaul, which changed homeowner deductions and credits, business personal property taxation and local government revenue rules.
A subsequent Indiana Fiscal Policy Institute analysis found that most homeowners would likely receive relief, but owners of low-value homes could face increases while more expensive homes received larger breaks.
State defends annual adjustments
Tim Rushenberg, general counsel for the Department of Local Government Finance, said Indiana can change its assessment tools, but the results must still meet constitutional requirements for uniform, equal and just valuations.
The department’s report explains that assessed value is only one part of a property tax bill, which also depends on local budgets, tax levies, deductions, credits and caps.
“An individual parcel can see a higher bill even when the district rate falls, or a lower bill despite increasing gross assessed value,” Rushenberg said. “There’s a lot of moving parts, so there is no reliable shortcut from gross assessed value to taxpayer impact.”
Annual adjustments, commonly called trending, help keep assessments aligned with market evidence between physical reassessments, he said.
Story continues below.
attachment_6376
 
Less frequent updates could reduce annual changes but allow inequities to accumulate and produce larger increases when properties are eventually reassessed. Limits tied to purchase prices or annual assessment growth could also raise constitutional questions if comparable properties receive different treatment.
Cost tables provide a common starting point for estimating property values, Rushenberg continued, but their results must remain open to challenge using credible evidence.
Barry Wood, the department’s assessment division director, said the state previously updated cost schedules once every four years. It’s moving toward annual review of the schedules or a related adjustment factor to help limit large fluctuations.
Rushenberg said the department wants construction costs, appraisals and other evidence to evaluate whether particular agricultural building schedules need correction. Public comments on readoption of the state’s real property assessment rule close Oct. 23.
“We want to look at the data,” Rushenberg said. “We’ve asked for data to see where, maybe in the cost schedule, something isn’t adding up there. But we certainly don’t want to make a general assumption that an entire schedule is is incorrect.”
Homeowners face hurdles, too
Rep. Cherrish Pryor, D-Indianapolis, raised concerns about longtime homeowners whose assessments rise as new or renovated houses elevate housing prices, even when they have made no improvements themselves.
She urged officials to make the process easier to understand and reduce the need for homeowners to challenge inaccurate values.
“We live it, and so it’s easy for us, but it’s not easy for the average person, particularly if you’re an older individual,” Pryor said.
Wood said assessors can distinguish between different types and ages of homes within a neighborhood when applying adjustments.



Quotation







Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences.


– Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis


Automated valuation models could help identify inconsistencies requiring closer review, said Hamilton County Assessor Kevin Poore. An assessor-led pilot is underway in Hendricks, Clark, Lake, Vanderburgh, LaPorte and Allen counties.
The department recommended beginning with an advisory or quality-control pilot, retaining local assessor judgment and taxpayers’ notice and appeal rights.
Still, Sen. Fady Qaddoura, D-Indianapolis, pressed for clear error measures and analysis of who would pay more or less before broader implementation.
“Anytime you bring a new model, you have to refine that system to be sure that there are no unintended consequences,” Qaddoura said.
Childcare funding debate continues
Also Wednesday, Adam Alson, director of the Office of Early Childhood and Out-of-School Learning, said Gov. Mike Braun intends to continue the voucher expansion supported by a one-time $200 million infusion announced this spring.
“The additional 14,000 CCDF vouchers are funded solely with state dollars and for one fiscal year,” Alson said. “The governor is committed to continuing this increase in enrollment, and as such, this additional investment and allocation will be reflected in its upcoming budget.”
September figures presented to the committee showed 46,579 children enrolled across the Child Care and Development Fund and On My Way Pre-K programs, with 17,732 on their combined waitlists.
Story continues below.
attachment_6393
 
Regulated childcare capacity nevertheless fell about 3.3% from a year earlier, to 156,151 seats.
Alson said the administration is pursuing regulatory changes and additional ways for employers, philanthropy and local governments to invest.
Whitney Coake, a Taft public affairs director speaking on her own behalf, proposed a “QuadShare” framework combining employer, taxpayer, state and philanthropic contributions. It would fund expanded childcare assistance, 12 weeks of paid parental leave and an early care trust fund.
Her model estimated about $1.74 billion in annual operating expenses, separate from proposed trust fund deposits. Financing would include a 0.3% employer payroll contribution and a 0.15 percentage-point increase in the individual income tax rate. Philanthropic contributions and investment returns remain proposed or illustrative.
Alson emphasized that communities need flexibility to develop approaches suited to their families and employers.
“There are places throughout the state that are saying this is important,” he said. “How do we figure out how we do it?”

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Sand, Lahn debate plans to tackle state budget shortfall while funding schools
text:
Iowa Auditor Rob Sand, a Democrat, and businessman Zach Lahn, a Republican, are competing to become Iowa governor in the 2026 election. (Photos by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch, photo illustration via Canva)Iowa gubernatorial candidates Rob Sand and Zach Lahn contrasted their proposals Wednesday during a televised debate on how to fund Iowa priorities amid both a state budget deficit and high inflation rate.
The debate, hosted by KTIV-TV4 in Sioux City, was the second time the candidates met on stage as they seek to fill the seat held by Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds, who is not seeking reelection in 2026.
Lahn and Sand spent less time focused on countering campaign ad attacks than during their first debate with KWQC, held at St. Ambrose University in Davenport, when Lahn, a Republican businessman who owns a farm in Belle Plaine, said his opponent was attacking his family and children by bringing his Iowa residency into question in campaign rhetoric.
At this debate, Lahn and Sand said they respected one another for their work as fathers and as people willing to take on the task of campaigning for Iowa governor. They also spent more time sharing their ideas, concerns and policy proposals on issues like education and taxes if elected.
Sand, a Democrat, repeated a pledge he made in the campaign to provide a 5% State Supplemental Aid rate increase for a K-12 funding in his first year in office. But he also sad he has told supporters and education activists that he “can’t promise that in year two.”
What to know as early voting begins in Iowa for 2026 general election

Sand said he could not make a promise for further increased funding in light of the state’s budget deficit. The Iowa Revenue Estimating Conference said in March that state revenues are expected to decrease by 9.3% from fiscal years 2025 to 2026, a greater drop than previously predicted. Republicans leaders, in control of both chambers in the Iowa Legislature, and Reynolds have said these revenue decreases were expected after changes were made to the state’s income tax system, but predicted that increased revenues through sales and use taxes, as well personal income taxes will offset the deficit in future years.
Sand was skeptical of this view of Iowa Republicans’ tax plan. He said he believed it was vital to provide a 5% increase to K-12 school funding in his first year in office, but being able to invest in the future — and in other programs he supports like “free school lunch,” would require the state to address the budget deficit and find new streams of revenue.
“We have to see where we’re going with the state’s budget,” Sand said. “That deficit, we’ve got to do something to address it. But, we could do that 5% increase, and if we are taking away tax deals for data centers, if we legalize cannabis, treat it like alcohol — the first year will probably see $50 million, but in years after that, we’ll be over $100 million.”
Lahn presented a different opinion on education funding. He said the State Board of Education should be given the ability to create “innovation zones” across the state, which he said would “give teachers and superintendents more opportunity to be able to teach in different ways to meet the needs of more students.”
“If you want to see what’s happening, just look at the rate at which teachers are leaving the profession in year one, two, or three,” Lahn said. “It’s just unacceptable. They want to help the next generation. So through innovative practices, we could actually create school choice within our public schools. We’ll have concurrent models of school that parents can opt into a more innovative method — not an experiment, something that’s been happening across the country for decades, oftentimes. That is an area that we really can focus in to increased funding.”
He also said “cultural issues” present a large problem for school teachers, who he said were being treated as behavioral specialists for some students.
“There’s 95% of their time is largely spent with 5% of the kids,” Lahn said. “And these are kids who, you know, from my own experience, having spent so many hours working with children, these are kids that are crying out for help. They’re looking for somebody to help them, even if they don’t know it. … We need to be the first state in the country to create non-punitive off ramps for these kids, to get them the one-on-one and small group help that they need.”
When the moderator asked if education spending increases must exceed the current national inflation rate of 3.7%, Lahn said the question was “not exactly the best governance question,” because work would need to be done to calculate how best to “bring more innovation into our classrooms.” He also said he did not believe measuring this cost against inflation was an effective way to ensure Iowa students are receiving the best education possible.
He pointed to phonics-based reading programs, a reversal from other reading curricula that taught students to identify and learn words using contextual clues, as an example of a way to improve Iowa schools without needing to put further money in the K-12 system.
“Making those changes really doesn’t cost us a whole lot more money at all to improve our rankings,” Lahn said. “There’s things that we can do that are very cost-effective to improve rankings. This is something I’m most excited about, is to work with our public schools to do that.”
Lahn also has called for fully eliminating the state’s personal income tax — and said he was interested in, over the long term, eliminating property taxes on primary resident, single-family homes. While Lahn has stated he would work to find inefficiencies that could reduce government spending to offset the loss in revenue from the tax, he also said there are other areas where revenue can be generated. He pointed to removing tax breaks for data centers — a proposal Sand also supports — and making more information on government spending publicly accessible online for Iowans to check and find inconsistencies.
“But I have heard people talk about, I think it’s a two-and-a-half cent increase in the sales tax would cover almost the entire burden of single family primary residences in the state,” Lahn said. “That is not my proposal, but it’s one option I’ve heard people float.”
Moderators added some levity into the debate by asking the candidates about personal preferences. Sand told the hosts his favorite flavor of pie was strawberry rhubarb while Lahn’s was Oreo cream pie. Both said pizza was their favorite school lunch.
Sand and Lahn will debate for a third and final time on “Iowa Press” Wednesday, Oct. 21.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico AG finds ‘substantial share’ of Project Jupiter public comments raise concerns
text:
A rendering of Project Jupiter with a public comment in which an Albuquerque resident writes that prior comments in favor of the development made under her name were submitted without her knowledge or consent. (Rendering courtesy of STACK Infrastructure)New Mexico Attorney General Raúl Torrez in a Wednesday letter to New Mexico Environment Department Secretary James Kenney said that a “substantial share” of public comments on the pending air quality permit application for the Project Jupiter data center were “not sent by members of the public acting on their own.”SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Source NM in June revealed how residents in New Mexico’s three largest cities said their names falsely appeared on pro-Project Jupiter comments after they were approached by canvassers representing the Oracle and OpenAI data center. Several elected officials — in the state Legislature and on city councils across the state — subsequently said their names were similarly misused, prompting Torrez to open an investigation.
Torrez’s Wednesday letter to Kenney said the New Mexico Department of Justice’s review is “ongoing.”
“As it proceeds, we will evaluate whether the conduct described in this letter may also violate New Mexico criminal laws, and we will expand the inquiry accordingly,” Torrez wrote.
In his letter, Torrez said his office analyzed all 17,419 comments submitted during the public comment period for the data center’s air quality permit application.
If approved, the air quality permit would enable developers to use a natural-gas powered fuel cell system to power Project Jupiter. Projections show it could emit as many greenhouse gases annually as New Mexico’s largest cities combined.
Torrez said that about 60% of the public comments — between 10,000 and 10,600 — contained the same pro-Project Jupiter form letter and came from 9,000 internet addresses, most of which submitted one comment apiece. Most listed out-of-state phone numbers even though the public comment portal didn’t require a portal, Torrez said.
He added that many of the form letters matched the supporter list associated with Project Jupiter’s website, projectjupitertogether.com, which hosts an interactive form letter titled “Send a comment to NMED.”
About 4,700 comments, most of which opposed the permit application, came from just 17 internet addresses, Torrez said.
Torrez wrote that he wanted “to be precise about the limits of what we know.”
“This letter does not establish who is responsible for any particular comment, and it does not characterize anyone’s intent,” he continued. “It does establish that a number of comments cannot be read as a measure of public opinion until the record has been verified.”
The NMDOJ review also turned up 22 comments bearing the names of public officials, local governments and organizations that all came from one computer, Torrez wrote, adding that “several of the officials named in those filings have informed my office that they did not write or authorize the submissions made in their names.”
“Taken together, these patterns mean that a substantial share of the comments was not sent by members of the public acting on their own,” he wrote.
Torrez asked NMED to preserve records including IP addresses and submission timestamps, to set aside the comments he’s flagged and to mark them as unverified. He also asked NMED officials to seek a ruling from the hearing officer presiding over the air quality permit application as to whether the flagged comments should be “considered in determining significant public interest.”
If the records can’t be verified, Torrez advised NMED to consider reopening its public comment period.
Torrez added that his office is asking Project Jupiter’s developers, its consultants and vendors to preserve corresponding records.
In a statement to Source NM, NMED spokesperson Drew Goretzka said that Kenney and Torrez met Wednesday morning to discuss the ongoing investigation.
“Secretary Kenney appreciates Attorney General Torrez’s investigation of this matter, and the New Mexico Environment Department will continue to preserve records in support of the New Mexico Department of Justice’s investigation,” Goretzka said. “While NMED has strengthened security measures in its public comment system, any person or organization that attempts to misuse the public comment process to steer a permit decision should be held accountable. NMED looks forward to continuing to work with the NMDOJ as the investigation proceeds, including helping in any resulting civil or criminal proceedings, as appropriate.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: AccelerateMS seeks $2.5M budget increase to expand staff and workforce programs
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Mississippi’s workforce development agency is seeking more state money to add staff as it launches and expands job training programs. The request comes as the state prepares for thousands of jobs to open in the next decade. 
AccelerateMS is requesting a $7.1 million operating budget for fiscal year 2028, which begins July 1. That is about $2.5 million more than its current appropriation, according to information that agency officials recently presented to the Joint Legislative Budget Committee. The increase would go toward hiring staff to help manage new programs, including UPSKILL (Upgrading Priority Skills for Key Industry Learning and Labor), which launched this summer, and the new Workforce Pell Grant program, said Courtney Taylor, executive director of AccelerateMS. 
The State Workforce Investment Board estimated in 2025 that Mississippi will face a shortage of 19,000 workers in priority fields such as manufacturing, construction and healthcare through 2035. Taylor said closing the gap will require the state to train more workers and students and to connect them to high-demand jobs. 
“The investment is crucial for our state and to meet the economy where it’s going,” Taylor said. 
AccelerateMS currently has 28 employees, Taylor said, and wants to hire an additional eight. 
One of those positions is a full-time Workforce Pell manager, Taylor said. The  Workforce Pell Grant program launched in July will allow eligible students to use federal Pell Grants for certain short-term job training programs. 
The expansion of the Pell Grant program, which traditionally helped low-income students pay for college, will allow students to pay for workforce programs lasting as little as eight to 15 weeks. 
Having a dedicated employee to review applications from the state’s universities, community and technical colleges seeking approval for eligible programs to qualify for Workforce Pell would help, she said. For now, an employee who oversees other federal initiatives, including the opioid-settlement workforce training program, reviews Workforce Pell applications. 
In September, Mississippi secured $8.5 million in federal funding to help launch Workforce Pell across all 15 community colleges.
Northwest Mississippi Community College will lead the effort, but AccelerateMS will help to coordinate and set up the program statewide, Taylor said. 
Workforce Pell requires a lot of management, including tracking data required by the federal government for students’ graduation rates, job placement and wage outcomes, said Iris Palmer, director of community college initiatives at New America, a national public policy think tank. 
The requirements for Workforce Pell “are very complicated,” and the process of getting these types of programs set up at colleges can be difficult, she said.  
Lawmakers will consider AccelerateMS’s request during their three-month session that begins in January, as they finalize the state budget for the next fiscal year. 
State Sen. Briggs Hopson III, R-Vicksburg, answers questions from fellow senators during a special session at the Mississippi Capitol in Jackson, Miss., Wednesday, May 28, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Senate Appropriations Chairman Briggs Hopson, a Republican from Vicksburg, said it is too early to know whether AccelerateMS will receive its full request. Lawmakers are reviewing agencies’ budget requests and the state’s major spending needs, including Medicaid, he said. Hopson said lawmakers will consider how much money the state has available and determine where it can be spent when developing the final budget.

name: West Virginia
title: WV Board of Ed. Takes Position the School Funding Formula is Inadequate
description: Charleston, W.Va. - The West Virginia Board of Education (WVBE) voted during its October meeting to take the position in a lawsuit challenging the constitutionality of the state’s public school funding formula that the current funding formula does not provide a thorough and efficient education to the public-school students in this State. The Board made this decision in a 7-1 vote, with one member absent, in the case of Patten v. Hanshaw, et al., in which it has been named as a Respondent. Filed in the Supreme Court of Appeals of West Virginia, the Patten lawsuit contends that the state's school aid funding formula fails to meet the constitutional requirement to provide students with a thorough and efficient education.Nearly 50 years later, the Patten case raises many of the same concerns addressed in the Pauley v. Kelly case, which examined the equity and adequacy of state funding for public schools before the Supreme Court and Judge Arthur Recht. Because the WVBE is constitutionally charged with the general supervision of public education, it was named as a Respondent in the lawsuit. Several Board members, however, have publicly expressed concerns about the formula and the financial burdens it leaves for county school systems to shoulder. “While it is the Legislature’s constitutional responsibility to provide for a thorough and efficient system of free schools in this State, our Supreme Court has held that it is this Board’s constitutional duty to ensure the complete executive delivery and maintenance of a thorough and efficient system of free schools. The current school funding formula fails to allow the Board to fulfill that duty,” the motion states.The formula relies heavily on enrollment to determine school funding. Many counties are serving increasing numbers of students who require specialized services, including special education supports. Federal funding covers only 12 to 17% of these costs, leaving the counties responsible for funding services such as occupational, physical and speech therapy, as well as skilled nursing care for students with more significant needs. West Virginia is among the few states that do not incorporate weighted funding into their school aid formula. This would provide additional resources for students from low-income households, students with disabilities and those in geographically isolated communities. The West Virginia Legislature commissioned the RAND Corporation to study the state's school funding formula. In its 2026 report, RAND recommended several changes, including revisions to the funding model. The WVBE has encouraged lawmakers to consider those recommendations and others as a means of providing relief to counties facing growing financial challenges. "The Board has directed the West Virginia Department of Education (WVDE) to assist counties through guidance and technical support to help address the financial challenges ahead," said WVDE School Finance Officer Uriah Cummings. "However, many of these issues cannot be resolved solely through reductions in force, personnel transfers and school closures. Several counties have already reduced expenditures as much as possible. The level of relief necessary will require a fundamental change in how public education funding is allocated." School funding documents are posted on the Oct. 14, 2026, meeting page.Specially Designed InstructionThe WVDE Office of Special Education updated the Board on statewide efforts to strengthen the implementation of Specially Designed Instruction (SDI). SDI is not a new requirement; it is grounded in the Individuals with Disabilities Education Act (IDEA) and Policy 2419, Regulations for the Education of Students with Exceptionalities, and is foundational to special education. SDI involves adapting content, methodology or delivery of instruction to address a student’s unique disability-related needs while also supporting access to and progress in the general education curriculum. This work advances the WVDE’s strategic goals by strengthening student outcomes, building educator capacity and supporting high-quality instructional practices. Ultimately, stronger implementation of SDI helps ensure students with disabilities receive the individualized instruction and support necessary to access learning, make progress and achieve meaningful educational outcomes.County Accreditation ReportThe WVBE approved the 2026 County Approval Status Accreditation Report, which serves as an overview of each school district’s operational efficiency and performance. It provides the public a better understanding of their local schools’ strengths and challenges based on 11 operational efficiency standards and indicators from the 2025-2026 Balanced Scorecard.This year's report demonstrates that many county boards continue to meet requirements across the majority of operational indicators. Several counties met requirements for all operational effectiveness indicators and had no student performance indicators requiring support or intensive support. Operational concerns continue to be concentrated in a limited number of areas, most notably Finance, County Board Member Effectiveness, Transportation, ESEA Programs and Special Education.Across student performance indicators, the most frequently identified areas continue to be Attendance, Mathematics Achievement and On-Track to Graduation. Several counties have multiple operational or student performance designations that warrant continued monitoring and support.The report also includes accreditation and approval determinations for West Virginia's public charter schools. Several charter schools continue to demonstrate challenges related to graduation rates, on-track measures, post-secondary achievement, attendance and mathematics achievement.Appropriate monitoring and support activities will continue in accordance with WVBE policy and charter accountability requirements.The full report and documents shared during the Oct. 14, 2026, meeting page. Learn more about the Balanced Scorecard indicators. Reminder: The next WVBE meeting is scheduled for 9 a.m. on Wednesday, Dec. 9, 2026, in Building 6, Suite 600, 1900 Kanawha Boulevard East, Charleston, West Virginia.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: State Question 847 would cap Oklahomans’ property tax growth. At what cost?
text:
Voters mark their ballots in the Oklahoma County Election Board on June 11 in Oklahoma City. (Photo by Courtney Bell/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY — A state question on Oklahoma general election ballots could slow the growth of property taxes, but it has raised concerns about the financial impact on public services.
If State Question 847 passes on Nov. 3, the assessed value of a homestead or agricultural property could increase by no more than 1.75% per year, down from the current cap of 3%. The fair cash value of non-homestead properties could rise by a maximum of 4% annually rather than 5%.
The state question also would add similar caps ranging from 0.35% to 1.75% for Oklahomans age 65 or older who make too much income to qualify for the “senior freeze,” which locks recipients’ property taxes at the value of the time they apply.
The ballot measure wouldn’t cut Oklahomans’ property taxes, but it would limit the increased tax costs property owners could face over time, which supporters say would give needed relief as other expenses rise. 
Others say the state question would slowly drain millions of dollars from schools, CareerTech centers and other core services that depend on property tax revenue.
Although the ballot language states the exact fiscal impact is “unknown,” the Oklahoma Tax Commission projected local tax jurisdictions would lose $45.78 million in revenue the next fiscal year, if the state question passes.
When extending that over 10 years, local government entities could lose out on $457.8 million, the Oklahoma State School Boards Association estimated.
OSSBA executive director Shawn Hime acknowledged nobody likes to pay property taxes “until you start thinking about all the things that you receive and the core services that are offered based on those taxes.”
“We have to have the resources available for core services like emergency management, our roads and bridges, our police and fire,” Hime said. “All of those things cost money, along with resourcing our schools so that we can have high-quality teachers in the classroom with every student.”
Oklahoma State School Boards Association executive director Shawn Hime speaks at an Oklahoma City Board of Education meeting Feb. 29, 2024, at the Clara Luper Center for Educational Services. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Oklahoma CareerTech state director Brent Haken estimated vocational learning centers alone would lose about $90 million over the next 10 years. Budgets would begin to constrict as inflation rises, he said, ultimately costing career training programs that help Oklahoma meet workforce demands.
“We will start to first be stagnant in program offerings, and then over time reduce because the cost of doing business will continue to rise while our cost of collections is not rising,” Haken said. “So, 10 years from now, you would expect to see less students enrolled in CareerTech than we do today if that measure were to pass.”
Local government entities still will receive more revenue than they did the year before, just at a lower rate, said House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow. 
Oklahomans have been asking their state lawmakers for relief from rising costs, which prompted the state Legislature to put SQ 847 up for a public vote, said Hilbert, who co-wrote the ballot measure.
Homeowners have been struggling under increasing home insurance costs and “through the roof” interest rates while “their house is getting hit with that maximum increase of 3% per year” in taxed valuation, he said.
“When you look at the national market of housing and interest rates, as a state government how much could we as a state do?” Hilbert said. “I’m not sure, but the one piece of that equation that we can certainly have an impact on is the property tax.”
House Speaker Kyle Hilbert, R-Bristow, left, debates a bill in the House chamber of the state Capitol in Oklahoma City on April 13. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Hilbert pointed to the expected $45.78 million decrease in property tax growth as an endorsement of the state question, not a drawback.
“At the end of the day, that’s $45 million that’s being saved to taxpayers, which I think is a good thing,” he said. “And so, I think that’s the crux of this argument, is the tax consumers who are against this bill are upset because they’re not going to be able to raise taxes by $45 million next year.”
The Oklahoma Farm Bureau, an organization representing farmers and ranchers, also has supported the state question. 
Agricultural properties sometimes lose money because of factors like drought, input costs, and fluctuating crop and livestock prices. Meanwhile, “property taxes on that land continue to steadily climb,” the Farm Bureau wrote in its voter guide. 
In Guthrie Public Schools, Superintendent Mike Simpson estimated property tax revenue generates about 30% of his district’s budget.
Bond issues, which also are paid through property tax collections, have been crucial in financing the construction of new school buildings, the cost of which has risen dramatically, Simpson said.
Guthrie Public Schools Superintendent Mike Simpson, right, attends an event in Edmond on Aug. 3. (Photo by Nuria Martinez-Keel/Oklahoma Voice)
Districts still paying back bond debt suddenly would have less revenue growth than expected, which Simpson said could cause a short-term increase in property tax millage rates. Hilbert said lawmakers considered this issue and adjusted the state question to mitigate it.
SQ 847 would limit districts’ long-term bonding capacity, Simpson said, and it would pinch school facility budgets that rely on property tax revenue.
“The relief (for taxpayers) will not be immediate at all,” he said. “It will be over time, and the net effect on the homeowner will be less advantageous to them than it will be a tremendous problem financially and a burden to the school districts and the entities that receive the property tax.”

name: WyoFile
title: Once they’re gone, they’re gone forever
text:
Does anyone remember when Wyomingites spoke with one voice and our representatives in Washington said, “Screw you”? I do.

Opinion

Remember The One Big Beautiful Bill? It was designed to reward the rich and add to our massive deficit. It did both quite well. It was also designed to sell off our public lands, an idea that more than 90% of Wyomingites surveyed opposed. Lawmakers from Montana said, “hell no,” and threatened to vote against the bill. So, the sponsors of the bill took Montana’s public lands off the auction block. 
What did our three courageous representatives in Washington do? They voted for it, without even a squeak. Fortunately technical factors removed that part of the bill, but U.S. Rep. Harriet Hageman has doubled down by leading the charge to get rid of our public lands and roadless areas in spite of massive public opposition from her constituents. And now she is on her way to becoming our U.S. senator, where she would continue her war against public lands and Wyoming sportsmen and sportswomen. Sen. John Barrasso will continue to sell us down the river in his own quiet way. If elected, U.S. Congress hopeful Chuck Gray will do whatever he is told by the Trump administration; what that will be remains to be seen. Our “true conservative” state legislators, like Sen. Bob Ide, are no better; they want all federal public lands gone. 
Do not be fooled by the argument that Wyoming should manage what are now Bureau of Land Management lands, national forests, parks and monuments. While the feds manage lands for many uses, including beauty and recreation, Wyoming manages state-owned lands through the five-person Wyoming State Board of Land Commissioners following one constitutionally mandated goal: to maximize income from the property over which it has jurisdiction. Just look at what the board did when it granted Prism Logistics a gravel mine lease on the face of Casper Mountain. Those beautiful state lands are used by citizens for hiking and general enjoyment. While the Natrona County community banded against the mine, the board leased it without considering the community’s desires. (The board later flipped its stance in the face of major public opposition to the project.) With that vote, they tried to gift the community an eyesore that we can enjoy every new day for eternity. The issue is on appeal before the Wyoming Supreme Court. Fingers crossed. 
The state of Wyoming lacks the resources of the federal government to manage the vast properties it would acquire if the proponents of the transfer were to succeed. The only solution would be to turn the land into money and divest ownership. Prime recreational land would be sold to the highest bidder so that some wealthy landowner would be able to fence and sign it off from us ordinary people. The rich would rejoice, as would the powerful mineral extractors, who would no longer suffer under the yoke of federal regulations. Of course, the less-appealing properties would remain in state hands, unless and until the land board could turn a nickel with them.
One need only look at the occasions when wealthy out-of–state “ranchers” from California or Texas have traded lands they have purchased to the land board for school sections of lesser financial value, with the exclusive goal of blocking public access to national forests or other public lands. If Wyoming gains federal properties, they will sell them off or exploit them — especially the desirable ones —  to our detriment. Imagine, “Mr. Musk, may I hunt on your so-called ranch?” I have fished in Colorado, where most of the land is privately owned. One either pays for the “privilege” or stands elbow to elbow with other fishermen on the few public pieces of water. We are so spoiled in Wyoming, we don’t even appreciate what we have. There is a reason out-of-staters come to Wyoming to fish and hunt.
Everyone should take the time to read the opinion from the U.S. 10th Circuit Court authorizing corner crossing to access BLM land. The decision turns on the federal Unlawful Enclosures Act. If the state of Wyoming succeeds in acquiring that land, the act would no longer protect us and corner crossing will become illegal trespass: a crime, and a gift to the landed few. 
Of course, it is not even clear that our national representatives want to put the public lands into state hands. My belief is that Rep. Hageman wishes to sell them off at the federal level, “to balance the budget.” Bull. That wouldn’t be a drop in the bucket, but once those lands are gone, they are gone forever. I am not an unmitigated fan of the feds, but on this issue I trust them more than the other side.
Is this really part of the Trump agenda?  Why do our representatives disregard what us Wyomingites think? Who is their master? Only one explanation makes sense: money. Where do mystery out-of-state campaign dollars come from? Could it be from persons who have plans for our public lands?
Cowboy ethics: “Ride for the brand.” Our delegation is truly “riding for the brand,” just not our brand. Let’s cure that problem when we vote.

name: Alabama Reflector
title: Doug Jones tells Montgomery town hall he wants to ‘phase out the CHOOSE Act’
text:
Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones talked about his education policy plan and other topics during a town hall in Montgomery on Oct. 13, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Democratic gubernatorial nominee Doug Jones Tuesday fielded questions about education and other topics at a town hall in Montgomery
Speaking to a crowd of at least 100 people, Jones talked about giving teachers and retirees a cost of living adjustment and said he wanted to “phase out the CHOOSE Act,” the state’s effective school voucher program. Income caps on eligibility for the program will end on Jan. 1.
“It’s (the CHOOSE Act) going to ultimately, if it doesn’t kill public schools, it’s going to just cripple and such that we do the public, and then we are seeing that in the numbers of kids that are in public schools this year,” Jones said. “The first year of the CHOOSE Act, 5,000 to 6,000 folks dropped fewer kids. The next year it was 12,000. Why do you think it’s going to be next year when the income caps are gone and we start giving handouts to people who make a lot of money?”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Alabama State Schools Superintendent Eric Mackey said during the Alabama State Board of Education meeting last week that preliminary numbers showed 12,000 students were unenrolled from public schools. Mackey said while CHOOSE Act recipients made up some of the loss, the large drop in enrollment can’t be attributed to the voucher program alone.
Jones’ plan to phase out the program differs slightly from his earlier talks of ending school vouchers in the state entirely. Jones said he “started out candidly talking about eliminating it,” but because there are students already taking advantage of the program, he wants to phase out school vouchers instead.
“Those kids made a decision and their parents to change schools and benefited,” he said. “They believe so, and the income caps were on, so we’ll phase it out. But we’ll let those kids graduate.”
Jones also said he was “committed to making sure teacher raises go up,” but that his focus will be split with ensuring that educators have access to healthcare.
“Healthcare delivery in this state is a challenge. It’s really in a crisis right now because of the cost of health insurance, the fact that we didn’t expand Medicaid, and it is really crippling,” Jones said.
The Public Education Employee Health Insurance Plan (PEEHIP) board plans to ask the Legislature for a $222 million increase in the fiscal year 2028 budget due to rising health care costs.
One public school teacher asked what Jones thought about the Ten Commandments being displayed in schools because of how it could impact non-Christian students. Gov. Kay Ivey this spring signed SB 99, sponsored by Sen. Keith Kelley, which requires local school boards to display a poster of the Ten Commandments in fifth through 12th-grade classes and within common areas, in April. The bill went into effect on Oct. 1.
“I think we’ve got to have an attitude in this state that is more open and honest about who our neighbors are and where they are and what they are and have that respect. The Bible that I grew up with, the Sunday school lessons I grew up with, taught Christianity, but they also taught respect for others,” Jones said.
A kindergarten teacher asked if Jones would be willing to split money in the Education Trust Fund for turnaround schools, an initiative to help struggling schools in the state, to provide for all schools in the state and bring back teacher’s aides if elected.
Jones said the RAISE Act, which aims to create a needs-based funding model for K-12 schools, is on the right path to ensuring schools remain funded.
“There’s school systems that have foundations that help them because their residents will contribute to those foundations, and I don’t think they should be denied state funding. I’m not saying that, but there are, and I think the RAISE Act is a real good start of identifying those schools and putting extra money there,” he said.
Jones also addressed questions about data centers, repeating his call for a moratorium on new data center construction to give time to develop plans for the facilities. 
“I believe that a moratorium would probably not even last a year. I think if right now the governor, the Legislature, whoever said we’re not going to build these things until we get it all together, I think people are going to come to the table, and they’re going to see what we need to do,” Jones said.
Jones used Lowndes County, which approved plans for a hyperscale data center Tuesday despite community members disapproval, as an example of why a moratorium is needed. 
The data center in Lowndes County, called Project Red Clay, is a 800-acre facility that would be placed near a residential area.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: In swift reversal, Minneapolis Public Schools superintendant cancels plan to close schools
text:
Lyndale Elementary Schools students board the bus after school on Thursday, Jan. 9, 2025, in Minneapolis, Minn. (Photo by Ellen Schmidt/Minnesota Reformer)Minneapolis Public Schools Superintendent Lisa Sayles-Adams said she would no longer recommend closing any schools next school year, less than a month after first proposing closures. Board chair Collin Beachy said that he would not allow any resolutions to close schools for the 2027-28 school year to be placed on the board agenda this year. 
The state’s third largest school district runs 59 school buildings for approximately 29,000 students. The district recently analyzed buildings and determined more than half are considered “under-utilized,” or 70% of capacity or less. The district operates its buildings with significantly fewer students per building than other large Minnesota districts.
The announcement surprised some board members, including Director Sharon El-Amin, who said she was “blindsided” by the superintendent’s announcement at the beginning of the meeting. 
After seven community meetings over the prior two weeks, Sayles-Adams said the community made clear the district should not close schools. Sayles-Adams said this will mean the district will continue to spread its limited resources across schools in ways that do not provide equitable access to opportunities for all students. 
The district has not named specific inequities, but in recent years, parents have reported elementary students without access to music or art specialists, and middle and high school students who do not have access to world languages, music or art electives. The district’s high schools also have varying access to advanced coursework. 
By closing schools and concentrating resources in fewer buildings, the district’s plans would have guaranteed all students access to music, art and physical education in elementary schools, and diverse electives in middle and high schools, according to Sayles-Adams. The plan would have also provided all schools with academic interventionists to support students who are not meeting grade-level standards. Currently, academic interventionists are only available at schools with the federal low-income designation of Title I. 
The district is dealing with long-term fiscal issues related to declining enrollment — state aid is dependent on enrollment — and rising labor costs.

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Advocates again ask South Dakota governor to endorse summer food program operating in 39 states
text:
A U.S. Department of Agriculture webpage explains the Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer program, which provides grocery benefits for families with eligible school-age children. (Photo by South Dakota Searchlight)Thirty-four South Dakota organizations and businesses have asked Gov. Larry Rhoden to support a program that offers debit cards for food to low-income families during the summer months.
The program is federally funded, but is administered by states. 
The governor’s deputy secretary of education told South Dakota Searchlight that the administration is “taking another look at the program requirements and associated costs” after years of resistance to accepting the federal money. The costs to set up the program and run it each summer “remain a significant consideration,” Deputy Secretary Laura Scheibe said in a written statement. 
The U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Summer Electronic Benefits Transfer program offers $120 per child, at $40 per month across three months, to help eligible families buy groceries during June, July and August. The money can’t be used for prepared food.
South Dakota would be in line for $6.8 million, according to the nonprofit Food Research and Action Center, enough to cover 57,000 kids.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Families could get the per-child stipend if they’re enrolled in the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, if they qualify for free or reduced price school lunches, or are enrolled in Medicaid, the federal health insurance program for people who have low incomes. The money would also be available for families who participate in the Food Distribution on Indian Reservations program, as well as for the families of kids without homes and those living in foster homes.
South Dakota is one of 11 states not offering the program this year The other non-participating states are Alaska, Florida, Idaho, Indiana, Mississippi, Oklahoma, South Carolina, Tennessee, Texas and Utah, all of which, like South Dakota, have Republican governors.
Iowa had previously opted out, but opted in for summer 2026. Wyoming also took part this year, so every state bordering South Dakota now participates. Tennessee lawmakers voted to fund the program this spring, but families there won’t be able to access it until next summer. 
To participate for the summer of 2027, South Dakota would need to signal its intention to do so by Jan. 1. 
Groups call on Rhoden to participate
Bread for the World South Dakota is the local chapter of a Washington, D.C.-based Christian nonprofit organization. 
The group sent a letter to Rhoden’s office last week asking him to participate in summer EBT next year. Among the 33 other signatories are the Salvation Army of Mitchell, the South Dakota Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, South Dakota Kids Count, the League of Women Voters South Dakota and the South Dakota Advocacy Network for Women.
Support from governor means state will cover gap in reduced-price school meals

The letter urges Rhoden “to help ensure that every child in South Dakota has consistent access to the nutrition they need to grow, learn, and thrive” during the summer months through summer EBT.
Bread for the World sent a similar letter to former Gov. Kristi Noem in 2023, urging participation for 2024. 
A handful of people and organizations reached out to Rhoden about the issue last year, Bread for the World’s Cathy Brechtelsbauer said, but the group wanted a more concerted effort this year, “because it’s ridiculous that we still don’t have it,” Brechtelsbauer said. 
“Everybody in South Dakota is paying for it through our federal taxes,” Brechtelsbauer said. “Kids are hungry here, too.”
Federal money pays for on-site meals across South Dakota during the summer, but Brechtelsbauer said those meals feed only 1 in 7 kids who’d be eligible for summer EBT payments.
“Not everyone is able to get to school in the summer,” she said. 
The EBT cards onto which the summer benefit payments are transferred can be used at grocers. Franklin Food Market of Sioux Falls and Team Buche Cares, the nonprofit arm of the Buche Foods chain of grocery and convenience stores, each signed the summer EBT letter of support.
State: Setup cost could be great
Earlier this year, Rhoden signed a bill into law covering the family portion of the price for reduced price school meals. His signature on the bill came after previous attempts to pass similar bills failed in earlier legislative sessions. 
The federal government pays half of ongoing administrative costs for summer EBT, but Scheibe, Rhoden’s deputy education secretary, said the estimated setup cost in 2024 was between $500,000 and $700,000.
“IT programming and additional staffing would be required,” she said in a Monday email.
The state House of Representatives Education Committee endorsed a bill in 2024 that would have put $150,000 a year toward paying the state’s share of program administration for summer EBT. The Legislature’s budget committee voted the bill down.
Dan Ahlers, the Democrat running against Rhoden for governor in the Nov. 3 general election, said support for summer EBT would be a given if he were elected.
“Honestly, that’s not even a question,” said Ahlers, who supports state-funded school lunches for all South Dakota public school students. “Of course I’d support that.”
The setup and administrative costs associated with the program would be “negligible” compared to the benefit for hungry kids, Ahlers said. 
“Even if it’s $150,000” a year to run the program, he said, “that’s nothing.”

text:
Members of the Alabama State Board of Education pose for a picture after its meeting on Oct. 8, 2026. Board members Thursday voted to approve a $6.8 billion budget request for fiscal year 2028.(Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)The Alabama State Board of Education Thursday approved a $6.8 billion budget request for fiscal year 2028, a 4% increase over the current year.
The request, which must be approved by the Alabama Legislature, includes increases for Struggling Readers Beyond Grade 3, school breakfast and transportation.
The Alabama State Department of Education last year requested $6.59 billion and received $6.58 billion in the FY27 Education Trust Fund Budget, the current budget. The FY28 budget will go into effect on Oct. 1 of next year.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“We want to make sure that every student, every adolescent is also a good reader, and that when they’re leaving third grade on grade level, they’re staying on or above grade level in fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth too,” said Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey during the meeting. “So when they get in high school, they’re above grade level going into those high school courses.”
The request is the largest component of the ETF, which funds public K-12 and postsecondary education in the state. The ETF this year is budgeted at $10.4 billion.
The department wasn’t given any money for Struggling Readers Beyond Grade 3, a program to increase literacy for students after third grade, in the FY27 ETF. Officials are seeking $45 million for the program from the budget.
The board also requested a $56.1 million increase (9%) for the transportation program for local education agencies and a $2.4 million increase (20%) was requested for parental leave. Mackey said during last month’s board meeting the increase was to help with the rising costs bus drivers face such as rising diesel prices.
The department wants to maintain funding in other programs. 
The department is asking for $58 million for the RAISE Act, which aims to create a needs-based funding model for K-12 schools. The appropriation would be the same as FY27. The RAISE Act aims to get additional money to populations such as rural students, students in poverty and English Language Learners. 
The request will come in a year where funding is expected to be tight due in part to health insurance pressures and uncertainty and tax revenues. Mackey said he doesn’t anticipate getting the full amount funded.
“We’ll obviously work with the new governor, incoming governor’s office, and legislature about what that number looks like in the end,” Mackey said. “The request is close to $50 million. I doubt we’ll get all of it, but I do think we’re making a good case for why that needs to continue to grow.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Scholarship tax credit vouchers, a wolf in sheep’s clothing
description: I have seen firsthand the disparity in resources among school districts in Fairfield County. This tax credit codifies and deepens those inequities.
text:
For months, governors across the country have awaited U.S. Treasury guidelines on the use of a Federal Scholarship Tax Credit set to launch January 1, 2027. Those guidelines have now been released, and the picture they paint for public education is worse than we could have imagined.  
The FSTC would release tens of billions of federal dollars to scholarship-granting organizations (SGOs) to provide services ranging from special education and autism support to private school tuition and high-dosage tutoring for students. Taxpayers who donate to SGOs would receive a dollar-for-dollar credit up to $1,700 per individual, or $3,400 per household, with no income limits.  

Joslyn DeLancey

The Trump administration has said that federal tax credit funds would not be limited to private schools; public school students could, ostensibly, benefit. The Treasury’s newly released guidelines tell a different story. 
SGOs act as middlemen for private equity firms, and the FSTC’s launch will provide these brokers with a strong, steady, reliable cash flow. The guidance around the FSTC tax scheme not only lets SGOs keep a 10 percent cut of every contribution, but it also gives them full decision-making power over where that money goes. They could decide every dollar they receive, for example, goes to religious schools.  
Under those same guidelines, states cannot impose a single guardrail on these funds. They cannot earmark them for students from low-income families or ensure they don’t discriminate. They cannot ensure these funds go where they would do the most good. 
The newly released guidelines only underscore widespread concerns about tens of billions of taxpayer dollars pouring into private schools and private-equity-owned education service providers. Education decisions would no longer be in the hands of public school parents, teachers, and boards of education; they would transfer to wealthy financial and tech investors.  
On the face of it, a $1,700 tax credit, especially one that’s reported to help all students,  seems hard to argue against. Look at the fine print, though, and you’ll see that it’s another voucher scheme designed to almost exclusively benefit the wealthy, direct money to private schools and service providers, and leave students and families with the greatest need behind.  
As a Stamford resident, longtime public school teacher in Darien, and vice president of the Connecticut Education Association, which represents educators all over the state — including Bridgeport and Danbury— I have seen firsthand the disparity in resources among school districts in Fairfield County. This tax credit codifies and deepens those inequities.  
Under this new initiative, high income families in Fairfield County will have the luxury of choosing to divert their tax dollars to private educational programs. These programs don’t have to follow the same rules, and taxpayers will have little to no say over what happens with those scholarships. There’s no guarantee of equitable distribution, and one thing is for certain: those dollars will not find their way to our public schools.  
Governors have until December 31 to opt into this voucher scheme, and those who care about preserving and improving the quality of their state’s education system will take a hard pass.  
We don’t need a crystal ball to know how this private equity scheme will play out in Connecticut’s public schools.  We’ve had a front-row seat to private equity’s destruction and abandonment of local hospitals and nursing homes, saddling them with enormous debt, stripping services down to the bare minimum, cutting core staff and resources, then cashing out and leaving.  
This has already happened with private equity-owned education service providers as well, including FEV tutoring, which closed overnight, leaving families across 30 states scrambling.  
For those who are undecided about the tax credit, the following questions are helpful:  

How do we ensure smaller class sizes, equitable funding, and accountability in our public schools under this initiative?  
Public schools are already underfunded by the federal government, especially special education. If tax dollars are diverted to public programs, won’t we pay for the tax credit either in property or state taxes to make up the difference? 
This program will create winners out of a few private companies selling educational services. Wouldn’t that raise the cost for services delivered to public schools? 
Fairfield County has some of the best public-school systems in the state, and we pride ourselves on that. Do we want to risk the quality of our public schools?  

Tax credits and scholarships may sound really exciting. In this case, you’re not saving money, and you’re not necessarily helping kids in need. You’re just playing a shell game: moving public dollars into private systems. Connecticut could and should do better. Imagine if we truly committed to investing in our public schools instead of buying into gimmicks.  
If it sounds too good to be true, it probably is.  
Say no to the Federal Scholarship Tax Credit.  
Joslyn DeLancey is vice president of the Connecticut Education Association.
